papers.title: Feasibility and Preliminary Effects of a Culturally Adapted Internet-Based Mental Health Promotion Intervention for Indonesian Undergraduate Students (LifeHack: Menjadi Mahasiswa Tangguh): A Protocol for a Single-Arm, Pre-Post Feasibility Study
papers.abstract: Background: Mental health problems are highly prevalent among university students globally and in Indonesia, yet the vast majority do not receive adequate care. Whilst existing digital mental health interventions in Indonesia have primarily targeted students with clinically elevated symptoms, no prior study has evaluated an internet-based intervention designed to promote positive mental health among Indonesian university students. LifeHack is an internet-based guided self-help intervention developed to promote positive mental health as part of the Caring Universities initiative within the WHO World Mental Health-International College Student (WMH-ICS) framework. LifeHack: Menjadi Mahasiswa Tangguh is a culturally adapted Indonesian version, developed through a systematic adaptation process guided by Bernal's Ecological Validity Model and the Heuristic Framework for Cultural Adaptation. Objectives: This study aims to evaluate the feasibility and acceptability of the adapted intervention, including its usability, participant satisfaction, adherence, and retention. Secondarily, it will examine preliminary signals of change in resilience, positive mental health, depression and anxiety symptoms, and coping strategies. Methods: This protocol describes a single-arm pre-post feasibility study involving 50 undergraduate students aged 18-25 years from Universitas Padjadjaran and Universitas Jambi, Indonesia. Participants will receive the culturally adapted LifeHack: Menjadi Mahasiswa Tangguh, a self-paced web-based guided self-help intervention supported by asynchronous personalised feedback from trained e-coaches. Participants may select modules according to their individual needs and complete the intervention over a flexible period of 1-6 weeks. Assessments will be conducted at baseline (T0), immediately following intervention completion or at the end of the six-week intervention period if participants have not previously indicated completion (T1), and three months after T1 (T2). Primary feasibility outcomes include usability, satisfaction, intervention adherence, retention, and intervention completion. Secondary outcomes include resilience, positive mental health, psychological distress, coping, and safety. Safety will be assessed through participant-reported negative effects and recorded adverse events identified through routine e-coach monitoring. Progression to a future randomised controlled trial will be evaluated using pre-specified traffic light criteria. Expected Outcomes: Findings will inform the feasibility, cultural appropriateness, and preliminary effects of the adapted LifeHack intervention for Indonesian students. Results will guide potential progression to a fully powered randomised controlled trial.

papers.title: Negotiating belonging and identity across the life course: A qualitative study using Social Identity Mapping with people with psychosis
papers.abstract: A core part of how we understand ourselves comes from the groups we feel we belong to. Having positive, meaningful group memberships, or 'social identities', has been linked to better wellbeing in people diagnosed with psychotic disorders, yet little attention has been paid to how individuals with psychosis experience social identities and changes in belonging across the life course. Personal recovery in psychosis has been described as centred on identity and connection: it may be useful therefore to consider the experiences of people with psychosis from the perspective of the Social Identity Approach to Health (SIAH). This study used Social Identity Mapping (SIM) as the basis for semi-structured interviews (n = 28). Thematic analysis, conducted by a team drawing on wide-ranging expertise (lived experience, clinical psychiatry and social psychology), generated four themes: (1) Pre-symptom social identity conflict and non-belonging: 'I'm just something in-between'; (2) Psychosis tears identity apart: 'The map would have been blank'; (3) Social identification is both a risk and a requirement for recovery: 'Everyone wants to belong to some certain group or another'; and (4) Lack of identification with people with psychosis: 'Do I feel a part of that group? Not really, no'. This SIM-supported interview approach uncovered new insights into how people negotiate social identification before, during and after psychosis. Social identification may be a protective factor, and social identity-strengthening interventions should be evaluated as means of improving quality of life and social functioning.

papers.title: Familial factors inflate the estimated effects of genetic liability to ADHD on behavioural outcomes
papers.abstract: Background: People with ADHD have worse health, behavioural and social outcomes, widely interpreted as evidence that ADHD causes these harms, justifying early identification and treatment. But ADHD clusters in families, and conventional studies cannot separate the effect of a person's own ADHD from the family environment in which it arises. We used a family-based genetic design to distinguish the two. Methods: We used up to 22 genome-wide significant variants associated with ADHD (38,691 cases, 186,843 controls) to estimate effects of genetic liability to ADHD on 16 health and behavioural outcomes. We compared population-based estimates with family-based estimates from within-sibship analyses of up to 164,220 siblings. We tested for heterogeneity between the designs, and applied sensitivity analyses. We involved individuals with lived experience of ADHD in interpreting the findings and shaping how the clinical/public-health implications were described. Findings: Population-based analyses implied that greater genetic liability to ADHD increased smoking, alcohol use and depressive symptoms, and reduced educational attainment, age at first child and cognitive performance. In family-based analyses, these effects attenuated. For example, the effect on number of depressive symptoms fell from 0.059 SD (95% CI 0.039, 0.080) to 0.002 SD (-0.052, 0.055), and age at first child increased from -0.045 SD (-0.058, -0.033) to 0.003 SD (-0.040, 0.047), with significant differences between designs (p=0.048 and p=0.034). Findings were consistent across sensitivity analyses. Interpretation: Much of the excess health and behavioural burden attributed to ADHD may reflect the family and environmental context in which ADHD occurs, rather than an individual's own ADHD. Interventions targeting the individual might not reduce these outcomes as much as expected. Distinguishing such effects requires family-based designs. Funding: Medical Research Council, UK Research and Innovation, Research Council of Norway, US National Institute of Mental Health, and Australian National Health and Medical Research Council.

papers.title: Interoceptive mechanisms of body image disturbance in anorexia nervosa: Study protocol of a randomized parallel-group trial
papers.abstract: Background: Current treatments for anorexia nervosa (AN), a dangerous psychiatric disorder, show only moderate efficacy. Interoceptive processing dysfunctions (i.e., how the brain receives and processes body afferents), and body image disturbance (BID) are clinical features of AN. Floatation-REST (Reduced Environmental Stimulation Therapy) has been reported to enhance both subjective interoceptive experiences and BID. The proposed project works to establish (1) how interoceptive processing dysfunctions may contribute to BID and (2) how the combination of Floatation-REST with psychotherapeutic principles may enhance interoceptive processing and BID in AN. Methods: In this randomized parallel-group (NCT06332963), single-site trial, 102 women and girls with AN will be recruited from an inpatient program. After completing baseline measurements, participants are randomized on a 1:1 ratio to receive either the interoceptively focused treatment (IFT) or exteroceptively focused treatment (EFT) condition. Both conditions utilize acceptance- and mindfulness-based principles, however incorporate skills that focus on interoception or exteroception, respectively. Participants complete acute measures following each experimental therapeutic session, as well as post intervention, six-week and six-month follow-up. The primary outcome of the current study is acute changes in BID assessed by the Photographic Figure Rating Scale. Additional outcomes include acute changes in interoception, and longitudinal intervention effects on self-reported, behavioral, and neuroimaging measures of AN symptoms, BID, and interoception. Discussion: If interventions demonstrate reductions in BID, mechanisms of BID will be further understood, informing the development of future therapies for BID in AN.

papers.title: Structural brain network organization and aggressive behavior in schizophrenia: a mega-analysis of 2260 patients and 3058 healthy controls from the ENIGMA-Schizophrenia Working Group
papers.abstract: Background: Although most individuals with schizophrenia do not show aggressive behavior, rates are higher than in the general population. Identifying the neurobiological correlates of aggression may inform prevention. Methods: We included 2260 individuals with schizophrenia spectrum disorders and 3058 healthy controls (HC) from 26 sites in the ENIGMA-Schizophrenia Working Group. The former were classified as showing at least moderate aggression (SZ+A; N = 231) or not (SZ-A; N = 2029) based on symptom rating scales. Structural covariance networks were constructed from cortical and subcortical volumes. We examined global and nodal network topology, as well as density within six large-scale brain networks and between each network and the rest of the brain. Metrics were summarized as the area under the curve (AUC) across a prespecified range of densities (K = 0.10-0.25, {Delta}K = 0.01). Group differences were assessed using pairwise permutation tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. Results: Global and nodal network topology did not differ significantly between SZ+A and HC. Network-rest density of the salience network (SN) was higher in SZ+A than in HC, although this difference did not survive multiple-comparison correction ({Delta}AUC = 0.018, pBH = .083). In exploratory subgroup analyses, higher SN network-rest density was observed only in SZ+A with high delusion severity ({Delta}AUC = 0.021, p = .007). By contrast, SZ-A demonstrated extensive alterations in global network topology compared with SZ+A and HC, alongside selective alterations in nodal topology and large-scale network density compared with HC. Results were broadly consistent across sensitivity analyses using alternative definitions of aggression and adjusting for current antipsychotic dose. Conclusions: SZ+A was characterized by fewer--not more--abnormalities in structural covariance network organization than SZ-A, which may reflect etiological heterogeneity. In SZ+A with high delusion severity, higher network-rest density of the SN may point to aberrant salience processing in aggressive behavior.

papers.title: Simulating Psychotherapeutic Sessions with Generative Artificial Intelligence: A Proof-of-Concept Study of In Silico Psychotherapy Research
papers.abstract: Background: Across biomedicine, in silico models increasingly complement in vivo and in vitro research. Psychotherapy science, however, remains constrained by methodological limitations, resource-intensive trials, challenges in manipulating clinically meaningful features experimentally, and a potential ceiling in efficacy. Leveraging generative AI and large language models (LLMs), we propose a framework for ''in silico psychotherapy research'': controlled simulations of psychotherapeutic interactions under reproducible experimental conditions. Objective: We test whether such simulation experiments can recover a theoretically expected effect of an isolated psychotherapy-process manipulation. Methods: In a preregistered proof-of-concept study, we generated 512 fully automated motivational interviewing (MI) sessions by linking locally deployed Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct based therapist and patient models across eight vignettes and eight therapist personas. Therapist, but not patient, prompts manipulated common therapeutic factors (CTF), contrasting high versus low empathy, affirmation, and alliance building behaviour in a controlled design. The primary outcome was MI treatment integrity (MITI 4.2 global ratings), assessed by a blinded LLM with repeated ratings and analysed using linear mixed-effects models. Secondary outcomes included observer-inferred importance/confidence rulers based on simulated patient utterances; Therapist Empathy Scale (TES) and Working Alliance Inventory - Short Observer (WAI-S-O) served as manipulation fidelity checks. Human coders rated a stratified subsample. Results: Of the 512 simulations, 506 (98.8%) yielded complete transcripts and 480 (93.75) were retained for analysis. Manipulation checks confirmed the fidelity of the CTF manipulation (WAI-S-O total scores {beta} = 3.14; [2.65,3.63], p<0.001, TES {beta} = 14.48 [13.92,15.04], p<0.001). High versus low CTF produced a theoretically expected improvement in all MITI global ratings, including the MI-specific features not directly targeted by the CTF manipulation ( {beta} = 0.54-0.95; all p<0.001). Simulated patient confidence but not importance for change increased more under high CTF ( {beta} = 0.17 [0.09,0.26], p<0.001). Human ratings confirmed the direction of the primary contrast. Conclusions: LLM-based psychotherapy simulations were technically feasible, demonstrated experimental fidelity, and showed theoretically concordant effects beyond directly manipulated constructs and simulation participants. These findings provide proof of concept for in silico psychotherapy research as a promising complementary pre-clinical experimental paradigm for hypothesis generation and testing to support accelerated intervention development. The applicability of this approach across patient populations, therapeutic modalities and model architectures requires further evaluation. Trial Pre-registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06813066; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06813066?term=NCT06813066

papers.title: Polygenic liability for major depression, schizophrenia and bipolar disorder and treatment outcome across major psychiatric disorders
papers.abstract: Polygenic scores for major depression, schizophrenia and bipolar disorder have been related to treatment outcome. We analysed 4,007 patients of European ancestry from 7 cohorts: three with major depression (STAR*D, GSRD, PANDORA), two with bipolar disorder (STEP-BD, Barcelona) and two with schizophrenia (CATIE, HSRRm). The three scores were computed with PRS-CS from the latest Psychiatric Genomics Consortium studies. The primary outcome was good response or good course, harmonized from each cohort's instrument. Firth logistic regression within cohorts, adjusted for age, sex and ancestry components, was followed by random-effects pooling. A higher depression score was associated with lower odds of a good outcome (odds ratio per standard deviation 0.88, 95% confidence interval 0.79-0.99, p = .04; false discovery rate q = .11). The estimate remained below one in all 8 sensitivity analyses, including adjustment for baseline severity, and was negative in all 5 cohorts with a continuous improvement measure. The schizophrenia score pointed the same way (odds ratio 0.93, 95% confidence interval 0.85-1.01) with no heterogeneity. The bipolar score showed no pooled effect (odds ratio 0.97), and its direction differed by diagnosis. In pooled data spanning three diagnoses, higher polygenic liability to depression was nominally associated with a less favourable treatment outcome, although the association did not survive correction for multiple testing; schizophrenia liability showed a similar directional trend. These findings support further evaluation of disorder liability in multivariable models of treatment outcome.

papers.title: Systematic evaluation of semantic similarity across language models for schizophrenia spectrum disorders
papers.abstract: Background: Semantic similarity features derived from language embeddings have been proposed as markers of schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSD), but prior studies have reported inconsistent directions of effect and limited evidence regarding their relationship to specific dimensions of thought and language disturbance. We systematically evaluated how language model architecture and preprocessing strategy influence semantic similarity signals in SSD. Methods: Speech samples from 228 participants (152 SSD, 76 healthy volunteers) were analyzed using six embedding models: GloVe, LSA, Word2Vec, RoBERTa, GPT-2, and Llama. Semantic similarity features were computed across three preprocessing levels (verbatim, disfluency-removed, and disfluency-removed with stopword filtering) using k-interword, moving-window, and sentence-to-sentence comparisons, summarized with various statistical descriptors. Features were compared between SSD and healthy volunteers and examined for associations with dimensions of thought and language disturbance, including inefficiency, incoherence, and impaired expressivity. Results: SSD was predominantly associated with increased semantic similarity across models and comparison strategies. Model performance varied by preprocessing. RoBERTa performed best on minimally processed transcripts, yielding the greatest number of diagnosis-associated features, whereas GPT-2 achieved the largest diagnostic effect size after maximal preprocessing. GPT-2 showed the strongest signal for inefficiency and incoherence, while RoBERTa yielded the greatest number of associations with impaired expressivity. Conclusions: SSD diagnosis and its dimensions of thought and language abnormalities are characterized primarily by greater semantic proximity in open-ended speech. Optimal preprocessing depends on model architecture and the clinical dimension of interest, highlighting the importance of model- and phenotype-specific analytic choices in computational studies of thought and language disturbance in SSD.

papers.title: Multimodal Prediction of Distressing and Persistent Psychotic-Like Experiences in Adolescence across Environment, Genetics, and Neuroimaging
papers.abstract: Adolescent psychotic-like experiences, particularly those that are distressing and persistent (dpPLEs), may elevate risk for a range of psychiatric disorders, yet the relative predictive contributions of brain structure, genetics, and environment to dpPLEs remain unknown. Using four timepoints from 7,399 children in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study, we developed stacked ensemble machine-learning models integrating cortical morphometry and whole-brain microstructural properties, polygenic risk scores, family psychiatric history, and childhood environmental factors to predict adolescent dpPLEs. Environmental predictors alone, driven by area deprivation index, neighborhood drug-related crime, and cumulative early adversity, were the strongest predictive domain (ROC-AUC = 0.687 {+/-} 0.003), outperforming genetic (0.619 {+/-} 0.020) and all imaging models (0.588-0.650). Adding genetic risk to environmental features produced the best-performing model overall (ROC-AUC = 0.697 {+/-} 0.007), whereas adding neuroimaging yielded no further incremental gain (ROC-AUC=0.683-0.696). Beyond environmental exposures, family history of psychosis, cross-disorder polygenic risk, and both globally distributed and regionally specific imaging components contributed to prediction. Childhood environmental factors thus capture a core predictive signal preceding dpPLEs, while genetic and neuroimaging features added comparatively modest discriminative prediction value, but may offer complementary biological insights.

papers.title: Posterior-anterior striatal reorganization after weight restoration in anorexia nervosa is associated with remission outcome: from mice to longitudinal human study
papers.abstract: Anorexia nervosa (AN) is a severe psychiatric disorder with high relapse rates despite successful weight restoration. Altered reward processing and an imbalance between goal-directed and habitual control within the striatum have been proposed to contribute to the persistence of maladaptive behaviours, but the striatal mechanisms underlying recovery and relapse remain unclear. Here, we combined cross-species structural MRI with longitudinal clinical characterization to investigate striatal alterations associated with recovery from AN. Mice with deletion of the vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChTcKO), a model of maladaptive eating behaviour, showed reduced dorsolateral striatal volume compared with wild-type mice. At baseline, women with AN (n = 71) showed reduced striatal volumes compared with healthy controls (n = 30). Longitudinally, patients with AN (n = 41) and healthy controls (n = 28) were reassessed, revealing substantial recovery of striatal volumes following weight restoration in AN. Posterior-anterior putamen gradient changes differed according to subsequent remission status, with changes in the right putamen gradient predicting relapse. Striatal gradient changes were also associated with goal-directed and habitual behaviour during the slip-of-action task, response consistency during delay discounting, and circulating ghrelin and desacyl ghrelin concentrations. These findings identify longitudinal putamen reorganization as a candidate marker of vulnerability to relapse and link striatal plasticity to reward-related and metabolic processes in AN.

papers.title: Ecological momentary assessment of anxiety and depression in individuals with early-treated phenylketonuria
papers.abstract: Background. In addition to cognitive difficulties, individuals with early-treated phenylketonuria (PKU) may be at increased risk for anxiety and depression. However, previous findings are mixed, potentially due to reliance on retrospective self-report measures that are vulnerable to recall bias and lose resolution of day-to-day symptom fluctuations. The present study used ecological momentary assessment (EMA) to evaluate anxiety and depressive symptoms in adults with PKU in real-world settings. Methods. A sample of 30 adults with early-treated PKU and a demographically-similar sample of 30 adults without PKU completed smartphone-based EMA assessments four times daily over seven consecutive days (nTotal=1,384). Anxiety and depression symptoms and processing speed task performance were assessed at each timepoint. Previous week retrospective measures of mood symptoms were also collected following the EMA period. Results. EMA compliance was high (82.4%). Momentary analyses revealed that PKU participants reported significantly greater anxiety and depression symptoms as well as poorer processing speed performance compared to healthy controls. In contrast, no significant group differences were identified using retrospective mood measures. Within the PKU group, Phe levels were not significantly associated with mood symptom severity or processing speed. Conclusions. EMA detected PKU-related differences in psychological symptoms that were not identified by traditional retrospective assessments. These findings highlight the feasibility and sensitivity of EMA for characterizing everyday functioning in individuals with PKU. EMA may provide a more accurate assessment of symptom burden and may be particularly valuable for studying rare clinical populations, where intensive longitudinal data collection can maximize information gained from relatively small samples.

papers.title: Cumulative Prenatal Adversity and Fronto-Limbic White Matter Development Across Adolescence
papers.abstract: Importance: The prenatal period is a critical window for intergenerational transmission of adversity, yet the neural substrates through which cumulative prenatal stress becomes biologically embedded in offspring brain development remain poorly understood. White matter microstructure is a candidate mechanism linking prenatal adversity to downstream emotional dysregulation. Objective: To examine associations between cumulative adverse prenatal exposure (APE) burden and fronto-limbic white matter fractional anisotropy (FA) at baseline and across adolescent developmental trajectories, and to test whether white matter FA mediates prenatal APE effects on emotional dysregulation. Design, Setting, and Participants: Cohort study using data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study, Release 7.0, a diverse longitudinal cohort of US children recruited at ages 9 to 10 years across 21 sites. After diffusion tensor imaging quality control exclusions and retention of one twin or triplet per family, the final cross-sectional analytic sample comprised 10 483 participants. Longitudinal analyses included participants with data at one or more follow-up timepoints across four imaging waves. Exposures: Cumulative APE burden, operationalized as a sum of six binary adverse prenatal exposures (unplanned pregnancy; early alcohol, tobacco, and cannabis use before pregnancy recognition; complicated pregnancy; complicated birth; range, 0-6) following Zhi et al. (2026). Main Outcomes and Measures: Fractional anisotropy in 11 a priori fronto-limbic white matter tracts at baseline (ages approximately 10 years) and across four imaging timepoints (ages approximately 10, 12, 14, and 16 years). Exploratory outcomes included Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL) dysregulation profile and Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (ERQ) subscales. Results: Higher prenatal APE burden was associated with lower baseline FA in left uncinate fasciculus (b = -0.00096; 95% CI, -0.00151 to -0.00042; FDR-corrected P = .006), corpus callosum (b = -0.00079; 95% CI, -0.00125 to -0.00032; FDR-corrected P = .006), and right uncinate fasciculus (b = -0.00071; 95% CI, -0.00120 to -0.00021; FDR-corrected P = .019). These associations were robust to adjustment for diffusion image quality, and prenatal burden was not associated with baseline image quality. In repeated-measures models across four imaging timepoints, higher APE burden was associated with steeper FA increases across adolescence (positive APE x Age interaction in 5 of 11 tracts; positive across all 11), though these trajectory effects were attenuated after adjustment for image quality. Post hoc analyses indicated that pregnancy complications and prenatal cannabis exposure were the most consistent contributors to these associations. White matter FA partially mediated the association between prenatal APE burden and involuntary emotional dysregulation, with no association with voluntary emotion regulation strategies. Conclusions and Relevance: Cumulative prenatal APE burden was associated with lower fronto-limbic white matter FA at the start of adolescence, an association that was stable across development and robust to image-quality adjustment. Evidence for altered developmental trajectories was more sensitive to image quality and should be interpreted cautiously. These findings identify fronto-limbic white matter-- particularly the uncinate fasciculus and corpus callosum-- as a candidate neurobiological correlate of cumulative prenatal adversity, while underscoring that this pathway reflects a bounded set of prenatal exposures.

papers.title: Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction for Generalized Anxiety Disorder: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo evaluate the efficacy and safety of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) for anxiety symptoms in adults with generalized anxiety disorder (GAD). DesignSystematic review and meta-analysis. Data SourcesCINAHL, Embase, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Scopus, SocINDEX, ERIC (EBSCO), and ProQuest Dissertations & Theses Global were searched from inception to October 2025; identified trial protocols were hand-searched for subsequent reports through February 2026. Eligibility criteria for selecting studiesRandomized, non-randomized, and single-arm trials evaluating the effects of MBSR on anxiety in adults with GAD. Data extraction and synthesisTwo authors independently screened records, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. The primary outcome was anxiety symptoms; the secondary outcome was adverse events. Random-effects meta-analyses were conducted, and certainty of evidence was assessed. ResultsOf 19 included reports (16 independent samples), 8 randomized controlled trials (n=1,012) were included in the primary meta-analysis. MBSR significantly reduced anxiety symptoms vs. waitlist (Hedges g=-0.88; 95% CI -1.57 to -0.19) and general active comparators (g=-0.85; 95% CI -1.15 to -0.54), and showed no significant difference vs. escitalopram in two linked trials (g=0.09; 95% CI -0.11 to 0.29), with fewer adverse events in the in-person trial, the only one reporting them (15% vs. 79%; number needed to treat to avoid harm=2). GRADE certainty of evidence was high for the escitalopram comparison and very low for waitlist. ConclusionsMBSR is a well-tolerated, nonpharmacologic treatment option for adults with GAD. Anxiety reductions were similar to escitalopram, with fewer adverse events; independent replication is needed. MBSR may be a viable option for patients who prefer non-pharmacological management or who cannot tolerate medication. Systematic review registrationPROSPERO CRD420251140213. SUMMARY BOXO_ST_ABSWhat is already known on this topicC_ST_ABSO_LIGeneralized anxiety disorder (GAD) is common and disabling, and pharmacotherapy is frequently discontinued because of adverse effects C_LIO_LIPrevious reviews of mindfulness-based interventions for anxiety pooled different programs and diagnoses, with inconsistent findings C_LIO_LIRecent noninferiority trials comparing Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) with escitalopram had not been synthesized C_LI What this study addsO_LIMBSR reduced anxiety symptoms compared with waitlist and general active comparators, although certainty of evidence for the waitlist comparison was very low C_LIO_LIIn two linked trials, anxiety reductions with MBSR were similar to those with escitalopram (high certainty evidence; g=0.09, 95% CI -0.11 to 0.29), with fewer adverse events in the in-person trial (15% v 79%; number needed to treat to avoid harm 2) C_LIO_LIIndependent replication and head-to-head trials against cognitive behavioral therapy are needed C_LI

papers.title: Early-Life Environmental Exposures and Brain Structure in Schizophrenia
papers.abstract: BackgroundSchizophrenia is widely considered a neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by premorbid alterations in brain structure. Urban upbringing is a well-established environmental risk factor. However, urbanicity is often operationalised using broad population-based measures, leaving unclear which features of urban environments might affect the developing brain. This gap limits progress in understanding the pathways linking urban upbringing to schizophrenia, an increasingly important question as global urbanisation progresses. Cortical gyrification is especially informative in this context, as it is largely established before birth and remains relatively stable thereafter, offering a promising retrospective marker of early-life neurodevelopmental disturbances. Study DesignIn this case-control MRI study, we examined whether residential environmental exposures at birth were associated with adult brain structure in 51 individuals with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder and 88 healthy controls matched for age, sex and socioeconomic status. Birth addresses were linked to geospatial measures of air pollution, green space, built volume, built surface and population density. Study ResultsHigher air pollution at birth was associated with lower cortical gyrification in individuals with schizophrenia, but not in healthy controls, particularly in orbitofrontal and inferior frontal regions. No comparable associations were observed for grey matter volume, cortical thickness or surface area. ConclusionsThese findings suggest that air pollution at birth may be linked to hypogyria in schizophrenia and provide a potential bridge between epidemiological research on urbanicity and neurodevelopmental models of schizophrenia. In turn, this work provides a critical starting point for future work assessing how early urban environments become biologically embedded in schizophrenia risk.

papers.title: Protocol for: Diagnostic trajectories of patients receiving unspecified psychosis-spectrum diagnoses. A retrospective, longitudinal, register-based study in a large UK secondary mental healthcare service from 2007 to 2024
papers.abstract: BackgroundUnspecified psychosis-spectrum diagnoses (ICD code F29) are commonly used when the underlying disorder remains uncertain, particularly at first presentation. These diagnoses may persist or later be revised as the clinical picture evolves, yet little is known about their long-term trajectories or implications for treatment and service use in routine mental healthcare. ObjectivesTo describe the usage and persistence of unspecified non-organic psychosis (F29) and other non-specific diagnoses, and the time to transition to a specific diagnosis. Secondary objectives are to describe temporal trends in their use, identify demographic and clinical characteristics associated with diagnostic persistence, and characterise treatment patterns, service utilisation, mortality, and discharge across diagnostic groups. MethodsWe will conduct a retrospective longitudinal cohort study using de-identified electronic health-record data from the South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust (SLaM), accessed through the Clinical Record Interactive Search (CRIS) system, between 1 January 2007 and 31 December 2024. The study population will include patients with an ICD-10 psychosis-spectrum diagnosis (F2x.x), substance induced psychotic disorder (or F1x.5), bipolar disorder or affective disorder with documented psychotic symptoms(F32/3.3). Diagnoses will be classified as specific or non-specific according to their ICD-10 category. Primary analysis will examine time from first F29 diagnosis to first subsequent specific psychosis-spectrum or bipolar diagnosis using Cox proportional hazards regression, with discharge from SLaM, death and administrative end of follow-up treated as censoring events. Associations with diagnostic transition will be examined adjusting for age, sex, ethnicity, area-level deprivation, route of service entry, and calendar period. Secondary competing-risk analysis will estimate the cumulative incidence of diagnostic transition using the Aalen- Johansen estimator, treating discharge and death as competing events. Ethics and DisseminationCRIS operates under ethical approval from the South Central-Oxford C Research Ethics Committee (23/SC/0257). Project-specific approval was received from the CRIS Oversight Committee as Project 23-095. The study will be reported in accordance with the RECORD extension of the STROBE guidelines. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publication and will provide evidence on the longitudinal use and refinement of non-specific psychosis-spectrum diagnoses in routine secondary mental healthcare.

papers.title: Developmental trajectories of child resilience, their determinants, and associations with risk experiences and behaviours: protocol for a national cohort study within the ReDiKid project
papers.abstract: BackgroundResilience during the transition from middle childhood towards early adolescence is best understood as a dynamic, adversity-activated developmental process rather than a fixed individual trait. Building on the Resilient Kid in the Digital World framework, this protocol describes the longitudinal component of the broader research programme, designed to characterise developmental trajectories of resilience-related capacities and resources and adaptive functioning, identify their determinants, and examine prospective associations with risk experiences and behaviours across behavioural, family, school, and digital contexts. MethodsThis is a national school-based cohort study following children aged 9-11 years at baseline across four waves at approximately six-month intervals from autumn 2025 to spring 2027. Schools are selected from the Czech national register using stratified probability-proportional-to-size sampling by region, municipality status, and area-level socioeconomic status; all eligible Grade 4 and Grade 5 pupils in participating schools are invited. The recruitment plan covers approximately 72 schools and 8,000 eligible children, with an anticipated 50-60% participation rate for complete child-parent pairs, corresponding to a target of approximately 4,000-4,800 linked child-parent dyads at baseline. Longitudinal planning aims to retain at least 1,000 linked dyads through Wave 4. Data are collected through child self-report, parent self- and proxy-report, and school-coordinator online questionnaires. Measures cover resilience-related capacities and resources, adaptive functioning and well-being, risk exposures, digital engagement, health-related behaviours, family context, parental mediation, and school context. Analyses will be tailored to the specific research questions and may include longitudinal and multilevel approaches complemented by reciprocal and person-oriented analyses. DiscussionThe study provides a multi-dimensional, nationally distributed longitudinal resource for examining how child functioning and resilience-related resources change together with risk experiences and contextual conditions during a key developmental transition. The design explicitly distinguishes resilience-related measures from evidence of resilience under adversity and treats digital environments as one interacting developmental context rather than as an isolated exposure domain. The cohort may also inform understanding of early vulnerability and protective processes relevant to problematic digital engagement, without treating such indicators as clinical diagnoses.

papers.title: Prevalence of DSM-5 eating disorders and associated impairment and service use among children and young people in England: analysis of a general population survey
papers.abstract: BackgroundEating disorders (EDs) typically emerge in adolescence and carry substantial morbidity. DSM-5 revised EDs classification, introducing Other Specified Feeding or Eating Disorder (OSFED) and Avoidant Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID). We estimated general population prevalence of EDs, including ARFID, in children and young people (CYP), and the associated impairment, which remains poorly characterised. MethodsWe analysed the Mental Health of Children and Young People in England (MHCYP) 2023 survey, a nationally representative probability sample. All participants were screened for possible eating problems. Screen positives and a random sample of screen negatives were invited to a second-stage assessment; giving an analytic sample of 1,738 aged 11-25 years. Associations with impairment, mental health difficulties and service use were estimated using survey-weighted regression adjusted for age and sex. ResultsAny ED affected 6.7% (95% CI 5.4-8.3) of 11-25-year-olds and was over three times more common in females (10.7%) than males (3.0%). OSFED was the commonest (3.5%), followed by bulimia nervosa (1.7%), anorexia nervosa (0.9%), binge eating disorder (0.6%) and ARFID (0.2%). Prevalence peaked at 17-19 years (13.9%). EDs were associated with lifetime self-harm (aOR 9.1 at 11-16; 4.4 at 17-25), SDQ-predicted probable disorder (aOR 14.7; 2.5), medication use (aOR 5.3) and mental health service contact (aOR 2.1). ConclusionsEDs are common among CYP in England and carry high levels of impairment, self-harm and comorbid mental health difficulties, particularly among 11-16-year-olds. Nonetheless, more than half of those meeting diagnostic criteria had no mental health service contact in the preceding year.

papers.title: Self-harm incidents and restrictive practice use in an acute female inpatient unit: a service evaluation of a continuous multi-system improvement approach
papers.abstract: BackgroundSelf-harm is a frequent and challenging occurrence in adult inpatient psychiatric units. The use of restrictive practice to manage self-harm incidents continues to be widespread within mental health environments despite increasing national and organisational guidance to minimise its use. Purpose/aimThe aim of this project was to introduce and evaluate a continuous quality improvement programme to progressively reduce incidents of self-harm and the use of restrictive practice. The project was set in a female acute mental health inpatient unit. The project sought to embed improvements in an inpatient units interventions, procedures, and culture and staffs mindset, and move towards a sustained collaborative and positive therapeutic and communication-based approach. MethodsA retrospective service evaluation design was employed to assess differences in the number of incidents of self-harm, enhanced observation, seclusion, restraint and rapid tranquillisation in the period following the introduction of a continuous whole-systems multimodal interventional initiative in 2019. Pre- and post-initiation data were compared (2017/18 compared to 2019/2025) to evaluate improvement and whether this had been sustained. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, including frequencies, percentages, and means. ResultsSelf-harm incidents reduced between 2017/18 and 2019, with a downward trend sustained between 2019 and 2025 (136 to 72 incidents respectively between 2019 and 2025; 47% reduction). A sustained reduction in the use of restrictive practice was shown in all domains pre- and post-initiation (2017/18 compared to 2025). Clinical implicationsNo one approach will successfully reduce self-harm and the use of restrictive practice. Approaches employed have to be multi-faceted, multi-interdisciplinary, collaborative, and blend together to deliver improvement. Sustained progress requires commitment to an iterative process of continuous collaboration, improvement and adaptation.

papers.title: Autistic Adults' Perceptions of the Adequacy of their Supports and Disability-Related Information: Instrument Validation & Preliminary Correlates
papers.abstract: Autistic adults face considerable challenges in receiving adequate support, from both paid/formal (such as from disability services) and unpaid/informal (for example, from friends and family) sources. Having adequate support can lead to better health and well-being outcomes. However, most instruments designed to assess adequacy of support were not made specifically for/with autistic adults. This paper presents a psychometric validation of the AASPIRE Adequacy of Supports and Information Scale (AASIS), a community-informed adaptation of a previously developed instrument (the Quality of Care and Support scale; Lucas-Carrasco et al., 2011), designed to be relevant and accessible to autistic adults. We also used the AASIS to explore correlates of perceptions of support in a sample of 798 autistic adults. Our confirmatory factor analysis supported a two-factor structure for the AASIS (factor one: Supports; factor two: Information). Further testing confirmed the instrument was invariant across several groups, including race/ethnicity, gender, intellectual disability, communication fluency, and self-versus proxy-report. Regression analyses suggested that the way in which participants joined the study (i.e., through community advertisements or via established healthcare/disability services) impacted whether they viewed their support as adequate. Additionally, a higher number of adverse childhood events and greater experience of discrimination were related to worse perceptions of support adequacy across both factors. Our findings support the preliminary validity of the AASIS across a variety of autistic people, though further testing is warranted. Findings also point to the importance of addressing the needs of autistic people who are minoritized and/or who have complex trauma histories.

papers.title: Patient-specific subnetwork connectivity predicts deep brain stimulation response in obsessive-compulsive disorder
papers.abstract: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) can be an effective treatment for severe obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), but response is variable, and objective, reliable predictors of who will respond positively are absent. In three individuals with OCD, we implanted intracranial electrodes across the cortico-striato-limbic network before DBS. Prefrontal gamma activity, most prominently in the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), distinguished high-from low-symptom OCD states reproducibly across days. Acute stimulation of the ventral capsule/ventral striatum relieved OCD symptoms and, in one patient, significantly shifted this OFC gamma signal. Effective connectivity from therapeutic stimulation sites to these prefrontal regions defined three patient-specific OCD subnetworks; the baseline strength of the nucleus accumbens/ventral pallidum-OFC subnetwork predicted acute and long-term DBS response. Imaging-based modeling of current propagation in stimulation-activated ventral capsule to the OFC tracked acute response, suggesting that this prediction could be approximated from imaging alone. These findings outline a predictive, subnetwork-level framework for personalized DBS in OCD. HighlightsO_LIPrefrontal gamma encodes OCD symptom state and persists across recording days C_LIO_LIAcute VC/VS stimulation relieves symptoms and can shift the prefrontal gamma signal C_LIO_LIBaseline subnetwork connectivity predicts acute and long-term DBS response C_LIO_LIModeled ALIC-to-OFC tract activation approximates this prediction from imaging C_LI In BriefScangos and colleagues mapped three patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder with intracranial electrodes before deep brain stimulation. Prefrontal gamma activity tracked symptom state, and baseline connectivity from stimulation sites to these prefrontal regions predicted acute and long-term stimulation response. Modeled activation of ALIC-to-OFC tracts was associated with response, offering a route to this prediction from imaging alone. papers.title: Accentuated Divergence, Constrained Expression: Autistic Traits Modulate the Creative Brain in Adults with ADHD
papers.abstract: BackgroundAttention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition, and co-occurring autistic traits may shape its phenotypic expression. Although creativity has been discussed as a relative strength in ADHD, it remains unclear whether autistic traits are associated with different dimensions of creativity in adults with ADHD and whether large-scale brain networks contribute to these associations. MethodsWe compared divergent thinking (DT) and real-life creativity between 65 adults with ADHD and 73 neurotypical controls. We used subgroup comparisons, partial correlation analyses, and multiple regression models to determine the effects of autistic traits (ATs) on creativity dimensions within the ADHD cohort. Guided by prior creativity-network research, we analyzed resting-state functional connectivity (FC) of the Default Mode Network (DMN) and Frontoparietal Network (FPN) to uncover the neural mechanisms. ResultsThe ADHD cohort demonstrated significantly higher scores on both DT (ps = 0.002-0.009) and real-life creativity measures (ps = 0.011-0.017) compared to the neurotypical control group. Importantly, increased ATs within the ADHD group were associated with a dissociated creativity profile, showing positive associations with DT but negative associations with real-life creativity. At the neural level, stronger right DMN-FPN connectivity mediated positive associations between ATs and DT performance (ps = 0.007-0.018), but mediated a negative association between ATs and self-reported imagination (p = 0.029). ConclusionsIn individuals with ADHD, co-occurring ATs exert a paradoxical effect on creativity, enhancing DT while compromising real-life creative achievement. In this subgroup with ADHD and elevated ATs, interventions should capitalize on ATs-associated ideational strengths while circumventing translational barriers, to enhance real-world creative outcomes.

papers.title: Intersectional inequalities in youth mental health measurement and outcomes: population-representative evidence from the UK Millennium Cohort Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundPopulation-representative evidence on social inequalities in youth mental health from an intersectional perspective is limited. We investigated inequalities across multiple mental health outcomes among young adults and examined whether measures operated equivalently across social and intersectional groups. MethodsCross-sectional analyses were conducted with 9,675 participants aged 23 years from the nationally representative UK Millennium Cohort Study (born 2000-2002). Self-reported outcomes included psychological distress (Kessler-6), probable serious psychological distress/ caseness (Kessler-6 score [≥]13), psychological wellbeing (Short Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Well-Being Scale; SWEMWBS), past-year self-harm, and lifetime suicide attempts. Measurement invariance analyses assessed comparability of the Kessler-6 and SWEMWBS across groups. Intersectional MAIHDA examined inequalities by sex assigned at birth, ethnic identity/background, sexual identity, and childhood poverty. Young people with lived experience of mental ill-health and/or social discrimination contributed to study design, interpretation, and reporting. FindingsLarge inequalities were observed across all outcomes, with the largest disparities by sexual identity, followed by sex assigned at birth, childhood poverty history, and ethnic identity/background. Across intersectional strata, predicted psychological distress ranged from-0.27 to 1.32 SDs, and psychological wellbeing from-0.54 to 0.11 SDs. Predicted prevalence varied 6.99-fold (9.81% to 68.55%) for psychological distress caseness, 6.84-fold (8.60% to 58.79%) for self-harm, and 22.10-fold (1.96% to 43.32%) for suicide attempts. Young people at the intersection of sexual minority status, female birth sex, childhood poverty, and some ethnic minority identities/backgrounds experienced particularly poor outcomes. Most inequalities showed cumulative patterns consistent with additive expectations, although some intersectional groups experienced better or worse outcomes than expected. Accounting for measurement differences revealed inequalities that were otherwise undetected. InterpretationFindings highlight the large extent of mental health inequalities when multiple dimensions of social (dis)advantage are considered, and the need to address both the social conditions generating these inequalities and the methodological assumptions shaping how they are measured and understood.

papers.title: Association of neurotransmitter-based polygenic scores with antidepressant treatment outcomes in patients with major depressive disorder
papers.abstract: Biologically informed polygenic scores (PGSs) may help interpret genetic associations with treatment outcomes. Here, we computed neurotransmitter-based PGSs (NeuroPGSs) for patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) and assessed their association with SSRI treatment outcomes. By targeting genetic variants involved in key neurotransmission pathways, we developed PGSs for serotonergic (5228), gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA, 4103), dopaminergic (7061), and glutamatergic (5690) variants. We leveraged data from two cohorts of patients who received SSRIs for at least 4 weeks: the International SSRI Pharmacogenomics Consortium (ISPC) and the Pharmacogenomics Research Network Antidepressants Medication Pharmacogenomics Study (PGRN-AMPS). Treatment response was defined as [≥]50% reduction from baseline depression symptoms, measured using 17-item Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression (HRSD-17) in ISPC and 16-item Quick Inventory of Depressive Symptomatology (QIDS-C16) in PGRN-AMPS. Remission was defined as HRSD-17 [≤]7 (ISPC) or QIDS-C16[≤]5 (PGRN-AMPS). The association between each NeuroPGS and antidepressant response or remission was evaluated using logistic regression models, adjusting for age, sex and five genetic principal components, with statistical significance determined at Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted p<0.05. The GABAergic-based PGS was associated with SSRI response (aOR per SD = 1.45, 95%CI: 1.14-1.85). Patients with the highest GABAergic PGS (10th decile) had 2.59-fold higher odds of response (95%CI: 1.46-4.60) compared to those with the lowest decile (1st decile). These exploratory findings support further evaluation of NeuroPGSs; independent replication and assessment of incremental predictive value are needed before clinical application.

papers.title: Event-related potential signatures of auditory predictive processing in first-episode psychosis: a passive pattern-based study
papers.abstract: BackgroundPredictive-processing accounts propose altered prediction-error signaling in psychosis. However, event-related potential (ERP) findings in first-episode psychosis (FEP) are inconsistent and focused predominantly on mismatch negativity (MMN). Examining anticipatory and later post-stimulus ERP responses alongside MMN within a single passive paradigm may broaden the assessment of predictive processing in FEP. Methods34 participants with non-affective FEP and 34 healthy controls (HC) underwent EEG during a passive auditory pattern-based paradigm. Mean amplitudes of contingent negative variation (CNV), MMN, and post-imperative negative variation (PINV) were quantified at five frontocentral electrodes. Exploratory analyses examined N1 and P2 mean amplitudes. Mixed models tested group, electrode, and group-by-electrode effects adjusting for age, sex and years of education. Regressions examined ERP associations with psychotic-like experiences, neurocognition, and social cognition across groups, and with symptoms, functioning, and antipsychotic dose within FEP. ResultsFEP participants reported more psychotic-like experiences and showed poorer global and social cognition than HC (all p-FDR [≤].042). Standardized adjusted FEP-HC differences at FCz were nonsignificant for CNV ({beta} = -0.46), MMN ({beta} = -0.30), and PINV ({beta} = -0.10; all p-FDR [≥].265). Exploratory analyses identified lower P2 amplitude in FEP at FCz ({beta} = -0.73; p-FDR =.019) and in the averaged frontocentral ROI ({beta} = -0.64; p-FDR =.027). No ERP-phenotype associations survived FDR correction. ConclusionsDespite phenotypic differences between FEP and HC, no significant differences emerged in the primary ERP indices of predictive processing examined. The exploratory P2 finding and its possible relationship to predictive processing and frontal dysfunction in FEP warrant further investigation.

papers.title: Focus or Feeding: A Quantitative Analysis of Prescribed Amphetamines in Human Milk
papers.abstract: ObjectiveAmphetamine (AMP) and its derivates are commonly prescribed for the management of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). This study aimed to 1) quantify AMPs transfer into human milk in lactating women receiving therapeutic doses and 2) contextualize infant exposure. MethodsMilk samples and dyad health histories of thirteen lactating women treated with varying doses of either mixed AMP, dextroamphetamine, or lisdexamfetamine were released for this study from the InfantRisk Human Milk Biorepository. Milk drug concentrations were quantified by validated liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) and used to calculate standard relative infant dose (RIDmat) and RID standardized to the defined daily dose (RIDDDD) of 15 mg AMP base. ResultsAverage milk concentrations (Cavg) of AMP base ranged from 23.3 to 297.0 ng/mL and increased linearly (R{superscript 2} = 0.92) with maternal daily dose. The RIDmat ranged 3.6-10.8% and RIDDDD ranged 1.4-21.8%. The fitted regression line crossed the 10% RIDDDD threshold at 1.17x DDD, with the upper 95% prediction limit crossing at 0.84x DDD. No adverse event reported by the mother-infant dyads were attributed to AMP exposure, notably including absence of reduced milk supply. ConclusionsThe levels of AMP observed in human milk followed a dose predictable manner. The average patient was predicted to remain below the 10% RID DDD safety threshold at total daily doses at or below approximately 28 mg of mixed AMP salts or 59 mg of lisdexamfetamine. Ninety-five percent of patients were predicted to remain below the threshold at or below approximately 20 mg and 40 mg, respectively.

papers.title: Shared Social Brain Gray Matter Reductions in Depression, Schizophrenia, and Alcohol Use Disorder: A Meta-Analysis
papers.abstract: ImportanceAnhedonia, social withdrawal and executive deficits represent transdiagnostic symptoms in depression, schizophrenia and addition, yet transdiagnostic brain volumetric alterations and their contribution to these symptom domains have not been systematically characterized. ObjectiveTo determine common and disorder-specific gray matter deficits in patients with schizophrenia (SZ), major depression disorder (MDD) and alcohol use disorder (AUD) compared to heathy controls. Data SourcesA comprehensive literature search using three databases including PubMed, Web of Science and PsycInfo (between January 2000 to March 2024) as well as searches on review articles. Study SelectionStudies had to be published in English, reporting whole-brain results, comparing patients and healthy controls. Data Extraction and SynthesisThis meta-analysis adhered to the PRISMA guidelines and was pre-registered (https://osf.io/s57uq) prior to data analysis. Data was independently extracted and verified by 3 contributors, and statistical brain maps were generated using Seed-based d Mapping with Permutation of Subject Images (SDM-PSI) random-effects model. 147 VBM studies encompassing 90 Schizophrenia, 44 MDD and 13 AUD studies were finally included. Main Outcomes and MeasuresStatistical maps of common and disorder-specific gray matter deficits in patients versus healthy controls are presented. Statistical inference utilized permutation tests, with threshold at p < .0025 and cluster extent of 10 voxels. Heterogeneity was evaluated using the I2 statistic and publication bias using Eggers regression test. ResultsCapitalizing on a coordinate-based meta-analysis involving n=13,041 participants, we found shared GMV alterations in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, ventral anterior cingulate cortex, insula, superior temporal gyrus. On the network level, we found robust functional interactions of the identified shared regions with the cortical midline structures as well as social and theory of mind-related behavioral functions. Subsequent characterization analyses highlighted the involvement of dopaminergic and serotonergic neurotransmitters as well as associated genetic annotations. Conclusions and RelevanceOverall, the present meta-analysis found common as well as separate GMV abnormalities in schizophrenia, major depressive disorder and alcohol use disorder suggesting a common neurostructural substrate and treatment target for social withdrawal and anhedonia across these disorders. Key pointsO_ST_ABSQuestionC_ST_ABSCan transdiagnostic meta-analytic mapping identify common gray matter alterations associated with shared reward-related, social, and executive symptoms across major depressive disorder, schizophrenia, and alcohol use disorder? FindingsThe meta-analysis determined transdiagnostic gray matter volume reductions in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, ventral anterior cingulate cortex, insula, superior temporal gyrus. We found robust functional interactions of these regions with cortical midline structures including social and theory of mind related functions, while transcriptomic characterization highlighted the involvement of neurotransmitter systems and shared genetic markers. MeaningThe study demonstrates regional-specific transdiagnostic brain structural alterations that may mediate social dysfunction and anhedonia across disorders.

papers.title: Promoting Community Living and Participation Outcomes Among Young Autistic Adults: Promising Results for an Autistic-Delivered Peer Support Intervention
papers.abstract: Autistic young adults experience substantial gaps in services supporting community living and participation. The Community Autism Peer Support (CAPS) program is a community-based intervention in which trained autistic peer specialists provide individualized support to autistic young adults pursuing self-determined goals related to community participation and independent living. We conducted a single-site, two-arm randomized controlled trial to evaluate the feasibility of implementing the CAPS program. Forty autistic adults aged 18-30 years were randomized to CAPS (n = 20) or services as usual alone (n = 20) and assessed at baseline, 3 months, and 12 months. Study findings showed that CAPS attracted autistic young adults with diverse demographic and diagnostic backgrounds, and most intervention participants remained engaged in services for extended periods. While the study was underpowered to detect statistical differences in outcomes because it was not a main focus of the research, a consistent pattern of results favored the CAPS condition across all outcomes. The largest positive signals were observed for overall and social quality of life, with additional favorable changes in internalized stigma, unmet needs, social functioning, loneliness, and positive autistic identity. Findings provide support for the feasibility and promise of an autistic-delivered peer specialist model focused on community living and participation. The consistent pattern of favorable changes supports continued development of CAPS as a person-centered approach to addressing outcomes important to autistic adults.

papers.title: Title Mapping the brain signature of dyslexia risk onto histamine, acetylcholine and glutamate receptor systems
papers.abstract: The brain differences of dyslexia are well described and its genetic risk is now measurable; the brain systems that connect the two are unknown. That link decides which measures complement one another in early identification and which systems intervention research should examine. Here we compared large-scale polygenic score maps of brain structure in dyslexia with normative maps of brain neurotransmitter systems. The structural signature of genetic liability aligned with the cortical distribution of neurotransmitter systems. The strongest and most consistent alignment appeared for the histamine H3 receptor, the vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChT) and the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) glutamate receptor. The alignment was most pronounced in cingulate, medial and superior frontal cortex and the paracentral lobule. The H3 alignment held after adjustment for cortical position and for metabolic and cognitive reference maps. Once the component common to all nineteen maps and position were removed together, no individual system remained significant, while the shared component itself aligned with liability. The signature therefore follows the topography these systems share. In 169 children, per-person alignment with the H3 map related to reading skill with the opposite sign to liability. To our knowledge, this is the first study to relate the structural signature of genetic liability for dyslexia to normative maps of neurotransmitter receptor and transporter density. It places that signature within the shared geography of the systems that set attention, arousal and synaptic plasticity during learning, and gives the genetics of dyslexia a testable biological axis.

papers.title: Dysfunctional Sleep Beliefs and Attitudes in Major Depressive Disorder: Dimensional Associations with Clinical Phenotypes and Gut-Neuroimmune-Metabolic-Oxidative Pathways
papers.abstract: BackgroundInsomnia is highly prevalent in major depressive disorder (MDD), yet the clinical and biological significance of dysfunctional beliefs and attitudes about sleep (DBAS) in MDD remains poorly understood. We examined whether distinct DBAS dimensions are associated with insomnia severity, depressive phenotypes, and neuroimmune-metabolic-oxidative (NIMETOX) biomarkers. MethodsDBAS-30 dimensions, clinical phenotypes, and NIMETOX biomarkers were assessed in 87 hospitalized patients with MDD and 31 healthy controls. Principal component analysis (PCA) was used to ascertain DBAS cognitive dimensions, and associations were examined using multivariable analyses. ResultsCompared with controls, MDD patients showed lower scores on "perceived consequences of insomnia," "sleep-related worry and helplessness," and "medication-related beliefs," but higher "causal attributions to aging or biochemical imbalance" scores. A composite DBAS score reflecting these 4 MDD-associated cognitive dimensions was constructed, labeled DBAS dimensional index (DBAS-DI). This score was lower in MDD and inversely associated with Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) scores, overall MDD severity, physiosomatic symptoms, current suicidal ideation, and recurrence of illness. DBAS-DI and the expectations domain jointly explained 35.4% of the variance in ISI scores, with inverse and positive associations, respectively. The DBAS-DI score was inversely associated with indices of the acute-phase inflammatory response, oxidative stress, fecal branched-chain short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and positively associated with serum antioxidant capacity and protective SCFAs, such as acetate, propionate, and butyrate. ConclusionsDBAS abnormalities in MDD extend beyond insomnia-related cognitions and are associated with illness severity, suicidality, recurrence, and NIMETOX alterations. These findings suggest that dysfunctional sleep-related cognitions are embedded within broader immune-oxidative and gut microbial-metabolic processes that may contribute to the insomnia-depression interface.

papers.title: Genetically regulated molecular mediators of phenotypic heterogeneity in autism spectrum disorder
papers.abstract: BackgroundAutism spectrum disorder (ASD) shows wide phenotypic variation, from adults without intellectual disability and with low support needs to minimally verbal children with intellectual disability and severe behavioral symptoms. Genetic studies of this heterogeneity have focused mainly on high-impact de novo variants and polygenic scores; here we investigate, at the molecular level, the role of common variants. Materials and methodsWe analyzed genotypic and phenotypic data from 9,332 individuals with ASD in the SPARK cohort. We considered 31 traits: six latent factors derived from the Social Communication Questionnaire and the Repetitive Behavior Scale-Revised, 22 co-occurring diagnoses, parent-reported IQ range, age at diagnosis, and age at first walking. We performed within-case genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and, for the 10 traits with evidence of SNP heritability, association analyses with genetically predicted gene and protein expression, splicing, and enhancer activity in brain and blood (xWAS). Nominated genes were tested for enrichment in biological processes, brain cell types, and developmental stages. xWAS-derived transcriptional signatures were compared with chemical perturbation signatures from CMap/LINCS L1000 to prioritize candidate drugs. ResultsGWAS identified seven genome-wide significant loci for five traits, including loci near GABRG3 and TENM2 associated with co-occurring sleep, feeding or toileting problems. xWAS identified seven gene-trait associations involving three phenotypes (FDR < 0.1), including CACNA1G with communication skills and NEGR1 with learning disability. GWAS and xWAS nominated different genes which however converged on synaptic transmission and gated channel activity, with preferential expression in neurons during later stages of brain development. PARP and p38 MAPK inhibitors were predicted to reverse the signatures of both social-communication and repetitive-behavior phenotypes, whereas several compound classes, including histone deacetylase inhibitors and mTOR inhibitors, were predicted to reverse the signatures of some phenotypes while mimicking those of others. ConclusionCombining within-case GWAS with xWAS nominates candidate genes mediating common-variant effects on ASD heterogeneity, provides biological insight, and suggests candidates for phenotypically stratified drug repositioning.
